claim: Participants' scan paths follow an active sensing strategy that incorporates information already acquired about the scene and knowledge of the statistical structure of patterns.
source: Using a novel gaze-contingent paradigm in a visual categorization task, we show that participants' scan paths follow an active sensing strategy that incorporates information already acquired about the scene and knowledge of the statistical structure of patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the gaze-contingent visual categorization task, including revealing density maps and correlation analyses showing that eye movements depend on image type.

claim: Categorization performance was markedly improved when locations were revealed to participants by an optimal Bayesian active sensor algorithm.
source: Intriguingly, categorization performance was markedly improved when locations were revealed to participants by an optimal Bayesian active sensor algorithm.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing performance across different revealing conditions shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The central process of selecting fixation locations is around 70% efficient in the task.
source: Our results suggest that participants select eye movements with the goal of maximizing information about abstract categories that require the integration of information from multiple locations.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling comparing participants' information gain to that of the BAS algorithm with matched parameters, as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A major portion of apparent suboptimality of fixation locations arises from prior biases, perceptual noise and inaccuracies in eye movements.
source: By using a combination of a Bayesian ideal observer and the active sensor algorithm, we estimate that a major portion of this apparent suboptimality of fixation locations arises from prior biases, perceptual noise and inaccuracies in eye movements, and the central process of selecting fixation locations is around 70% efficient in our task.
evidence: The claim is supported by model fitting and simulations showing that when BAS operates with participants' prior biases, perceptual noise, and saccadic inaccuracies, the discrepancy between BAS and participants is markedly reduced.

claim: Humans and other animals direct their sensors to extract task-relevant information efficiently.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that humans and other animals direct their sensors (e.g. their eyes, whiskers, or hands) so as to extract task-relevant information efficiently (Yarbus, 1967; Kleinfeld et al., 2006; Lederman and Klatzky, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The pattern of eye movements used to scan a scene depends on the type of information sought.
source: Indeed, in vision, the pattern of eye movements used to scan a scene depends on the type of information sought (Hayhoe and Ballard, 2005; Rothkopf et al., 2007), and has been implied to follow from an active strategy (Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Renninger et al., 2007; Navalpakkam et al., 2010; Nelson and Cottrell, 2007; Toscani et al., 2013; Chukoskie et al., 2013) in which each saccade depends on the information gathered about the current visual scene and prior knowledge about scene statistics.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous research studies.

claim: No studies have shown whether the information acquired by each individual fixation is being optimized.
source: However, until now, studies of such active sensing have either been limited to search tasks or to qualitative descriptions of the active sensing process. In particular, no studies have shown whether the information acquired by each individual fixation is being optimized.
evidence: The claim is based on a review of existing literature and identifies a gap in previous research.

claim: In visual search, there is often a single location in the scene that has all the necessary information (the target).
source: This is in contrast with studies that attempted to quantify the general informativeness of single locations in a scene (Gosselin and Schyns, 2001), and showed that they are the target of fixations humans tend to choose in general (Peterson and Eckstein, 2012; Toscani et al., 2013; Chukoskie et al., 2013), or visual search in which, by the nature of the task, the target location is fully informative by itself (Najemnik and Geisler, 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about visual search tasks and is supported by citations.

claim: Eye movements in visual search are well described by the simple mechanism of inhibition of return.
source: This is in contrast with studies that attempted to quantify the general informativeness of single locations in a scene (Gosselin and Schyns, 2001), and showed that they are the target of fixations humans tend to choose in general (Peterson and Eckstein, 2012; Toscani et al., 2013; Chukoskie et al., 2013), or visual search in which, by the nature of the task, the target location is fully informative by itself (Najemnik and Geisler, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Klein (2000) and represents established knowledge about visual search mechanisms.

claim: Some basic-level categorization tasks can be solved in a single fixation.
source: While some basic-level categorization tasks can be solved in a single fixation (Thorpe et al., 1996; Li et al., 2002), many situations require multiple fixations to extract several details at different locations to make a decision.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Many situations require multiple fixations to extract several details at different locations to make a decision.
source: While some basic-level categorization tasks can be solved in a single fixation (Thorpe et al., 1996; Li et al., 2002), many situations require multiple fixations to extract several details at different locations to make a decision.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about visual perception and is contrasted with single-fixation tasks.

claim: When people extract abstract information, they need to integrate a series of detailed observations across the scene, relying heavily on foveal vision information with peripheral vision playing a more minor role.
source: Therefore, when people have to extract abstract information (eg., how long the visitor has been away) they need to integrate a series of detailed observations (such as facial expression, postures and gestures of the people) across the scene, relying heavily on foveal vision information with peripheral vision playing a more minor role (Levi, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Levi (2008) and represents established knowledge about visual perception.

claim: Categorization performance improved with the number of revealings for each participant.
source: In the free-scan (active) condition, categorization performance improved with the number of revealings for each participant (Figure 2C, red points), indicating the successful integration of information across a large number of fixations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The inter-saccadic intervals in the experiment (mean 408 ms) were similar though somewhat shorter than those recorded for everyday activities (mean 497 ms).
source: Although we used a gaze-contingent display, the task still allowed participants to employ natural every-day eye movement strategies, consistent with the inter-saccadic intervals (mean 408 ms) and relative saccade size (0.75–3.9 normalized by the three different relevant length scales of the stimuli) that were similar though somewhat shorter than those recorded for everyday activities (e.g. tea making; mean inter-saccadic interval 497 ms, and 0.95–19 relative saccade size normalized by the size of different fixated objects; Hayhoe et al., 2003; Land and Tatler, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements compared to cited literature values.

claim: The pattern of revealings strongly depended on image type.
source: Importantly, we found that the pattern of revealings strongly depended on image type (Figure 3A, first four rows).
evidence: The claim is supported by revealing density maps shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Eye movement patterns for images of the same type were positively correlated for each participant (p<0.001 in all cases).
source: The pattern of eye movements for images of the same type were positively correlated for each participant (Figure 3B, left, orange bars; p<0.001 in all cases), whereas eye movements for images of different types were negatively correlated (Figure 3B, left, purple bars; p<0.001 in all cases).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Eye movements for images of different types were negatively correlated (p<0.001 in all cases).
source: The pattern of eye movements for images of the same type were positively correlated for each participant (Figure 3B, left, orange bars; p<0.001 in all cases), whereas eye movements for images of different types were negatively correlated (Figure 3B, left, purple bars; p<0.001 in all cases).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Eye movement patterns became increasingly differentiated over the course of the trial as progressively more of the image was revealed.
source: We also found that eye movement patterns became increasingly differentiated over the course of the trial as progressively more of the image was revealed (Figure 3B, left, curves).
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing correlations as a function of revealing number in Figure 3B.

claim: The dependence of the eye movement patterns on the underlying image type shows that participants employed an active sensing strategy.
source: The dependence of the eye movement patterns on the underlying image type shows that participants employed an active sensing strategy.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing image-type-dependent eye movements.

claim: When the revealings were drawn randomly from an isotropic Gaussian centered on the image, performance was substantially impaired.
source: To assess whether this active strategy used by our participants contributed to performance improvement, we examined the same participants in a passive revealing condition. When the revealings were drawn randomly from an isotropic Gaussian centered on the image, performance was substantially impaired (Figure 2C, blue points), indicating that participants' decision performance benefited from their active sensing strategy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing active and passive conditions shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Participants' decision performance benefited from their active sensing strategy.
source: When the revealings were drawn randomly from an isotropic Gaussian centered on the image, performance was substantially impaired (Figure 2C, blue points), indicating that participants' decision performance benefited from their active sensing strategy.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from comparing performance between active and passive revealing conditions.

claim: After the final revealing, participants rescanned on average for 5.0 s in the active condition and 6.4 s in the passive random condition before making a decision.
source: After the final revealing, participants rescanned only briefly, on average for 5.0 s in the active condition, 6.4 s in the passive random condition before making a decision.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of rescanning times.

claim: Participants' performance did not improve with increased rescanning time; instead it correlated negatively with rescanning time for 2 out of 3 participants.
source: Moreover, their performance did not improve with increased rescanning time, instead it correlated negatively with rescanning time for 2 out of 3 participants, such that the probability of a correct decision for rescanning times at the 25th and 75th percentiles of the rescanning time distribution fell from 0.77 to 0.54 (p<0.001) and from 0.77 to 0.66 (p<0.03), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the relationship between rescanning time and performance.

claim: Longer rescanning times indicate when participants are uncertain rather than providing the main source of information for their decisions.
source: This suggests that longer rescanning times indicate when participants are uncertain rather than providing the main source of information for their decisions.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the negative correlation between rescanning time and performance.

claim: Additional revealings during the original scanning period clearly benefit performance when chosen appropriately.
source: This is in contrast to additional revealings during the original scanning period which clearly benefit performance when chosen appropriately (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by performance data as a function of revealing number shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The revealing density maps for participants who were not allowed to rescan were very similar to the maps of participants who were allowed to rescan (average within-type vs. across-type correlation across the two groups: 0.63 vs. −0.30).
source: The revealing density maps for these participants were very similar to the maps of participants who were allowed to rescan (average within-type vs. across-type correlation across the two groups of participants: 0.63 vs. −0.30) and performance was also similar (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), although as expected slightly worse without rescanning.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis comparing the two groups of participants.

claim: Allowing rescanning did not substantially change participants' revealing strategy.
source: This confirms that allowing rescanning did not substantially change participants' revealing strategy.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from comparing participants with and without rescanning allowed.

claim: The best ideal observer model (4 parameters in total) provided a close match to the participants' performance both in the active and passive random-revealing conditions.
source: The best model (4 parameters in total) provided a close match to the participants' performance both in the active and passive random-revealing conditions (Figure 2C, red and blue lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Participants' active revealings were 2.93 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.60–3.32) times more efficient than random revealings.
source: Participants' active revealings (Figure 5A–B, red lines) were 2.93 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.60–3.32) times more efficient than random revealings (Figure 5A, blue lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by information gain analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Participants' revealings were 1.81–1.92 times more efficient than three heuristic strategies.
source: Participants' active revealings (red lines, as in A) were 1.81 (95% CI, 1.68–1.94), 1.85 (95% CI, 1.72–1.99), and 1.92 (95% CI, 1.74–2.04) times more efficient in gathering information than these heuristics, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by information gain analysis comparing participants to heuristic strategies shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Participants' active revealings were less efficient by a factor of 2.48 (95% CI, 2.33–2.62) than the information provided by revealings generated by the BAS algorithm with 'idealized' parameters.
source: However, participants' active revealings were less efficient by a factor of 2.48 (95% CI, 2.33–2.62) than the information provided by revealings generated by the BAS algorithm with 'idealized' parameters: minimal perception noise (2–3 times lower than our participants'; see Materials and methods) and no prior biases or saccadic inaccuracies (Figure 5A, black lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by information gain analysis comparing participants to ideal BAS shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the passive ideal BAS condition, participants only rescanned the revealed locations for an average of 4.4 s after the final revealing, less than in the active and passive random conditions.
source: In this condition, participants only rescanned the revealed locations for a short amount of time after the final revealing (average of 4.4 s), less than in the active and passive random conditions, thus their increased efficiency could not be attributed to longer rescanning times.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of rescanning times.

claim: When BAS operated with participants' prior biases, perceptual noise and typical saccadic inaccuracies, the discrepancy between the informativeness of BAS-generated revealings compared to that of participants' revealings was markedly reduced (BAS/free-scan efficiency = 1.45, 95% CI, 1.37–1.53).
source: Importantly, when we computed the information gain provided by BAS when operating with participants' prior biases, perceptual noise and the typical saccadic inaccuracies as described above, the discrepancy between the informativeness of BAS-generated revealings compared to that of participants' revealings was markedly reduced (Figure 5A, green lines, BAS/free-scan efficiency = 1.45, 95% CI, 1.37–1.53).
evidence: The claim is supported by information gain analysis with matched BAS parameters shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Efficiency remained stable over the whole course of the experiment, suggesting there was minimal, if any, learning required in the free-scan task.
source: To examine the role of learning in participants' active sensing strategy, we computed the relative efficiency of each of the free-scan sessions of our experiment, spanning multiple days, compared to the final session (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). We found that efficiency remained stable over the whole course of the experiment, suggesting there was minimal, if any, learning required in the free-scan task.
evidence: The claim is supported by efficiency analysis across sessions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Participants' eye movements were substantially more efficient than heuristic strategies that only employed a subset of the elements of a fully closed-loop active sensing strategy.
source: In particular, our participants' eye movements were substantially more efficient than heuristic strategies that only employed a subset of the elements of a fully closed-loop active sensing strategy, and were about 70% as efficient as the optimal active sensor that operated with the participants' own prior bias, perception noise, and saccadic inaccuracies.
evidence: The claim is supported by information gain analysis comparing participants to heuristic strategies shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Participants' eye movements were about 70% as efficient as the optimal active sensor that operated with the participants' own prior bias, perception noise, and saccadic inaccuracies.
source: In particular, our participants' eye movements were substantially more efficient than heuristic strategies that only employed a subset of the elements of a fully closed-loop active sensing strategy, and were about 70% as efficient as the optimal active sensor that operated with the participants' own prior bias, perception noise, and saccadic inaccuracies.
evidence: The claim is supported by information gain analysis comparing participants to matched BAS shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The 30% inefficiency found may be due to unmodeled constraints in human eye movement strategies, such as biases for cardinal directions or fixating the centre of an image.
source: The 30% inefficiency we found may be due to unmodeled constraints in human eye movement strategies, such as the biases for cardinal directions or fixating the centre of an image that were apparent in our data (Figure 3A) and that may also be beneficial in natural environments (Tatler and Vincent, 2008; 2009).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about potential sources of the observed inefficiency, supported by observed biases in the data and citations.

claim: Biases for cardinal directions or fixating the centre of an image may be beneficial in natural environments.
source: The 30% inefficiency we found may be due to unmodeled constraints in human eye movement strategies, such as the biases for cardinal directions or fixating the centre of an image that were apparent in our data (Figure 3A) and that may also be beneficial in natural environments (Tatler and Vincent, 2008; 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The estimate of 70% efficiency would become a lower bound on the efficiency of the planning process if biases for cardinal directions or locations turn out to be part of the execution process.
source: Therefore, as we were interested in the degree of (sub)optimality of the planning component, we chose not to factor out potential biases for cardinal directions or locations. Should such suboptimalities turn out to be part of the execution process, then our estimate of 70% would become a lower bound on the efficiency of the planning process.
evidence: The claim is a logical inference about the interpretation of the efficiency estimate under different assumptions.

claim: In one study using a simple object localization task, the choice of fixation locations was close to random despite obvious learning of the underlying stimulus statistics.
source: Our results contrast with recent studies suggesting that the pattern of eye movements do not follow an active sensing strategy. In one study, using a simple object localization task, it was found that the choice of fixation locations was close to random despite obvious learning of the underlying stimulus statistics (Holm et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Holm et al. (2012).

claim: In a study using a simplified visual search task, participants' eye movements were virtually unaffected by the configuration of the visual stimuli presented in the trial.
source: In another study, using a simplified visual search task, participants' eye movements were virtually unaffected by the configuration of the visual stimuli presented in the trial (Morvan and Maloney, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Morvan and Maloney (2012).

claim: Participants used both their prior knowledge of stimulus statistics as well as evidence accumulated about the current visual scene to guide their eye movements.
source: In contrast, we found that participants used both their prior knowledge of stimulus statistics as well as evidence accumulated about the current visual scene to guide their eye movements.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing image-type-dependent eye movements and correlation with BAS predictions.

claim: Better performance in the current study may be due to the more naturalistic task, which involves the extraction of abstract latent features, revealing more typical processing of the sensorimotor system.
source: We speculate that better performance in our case may be due to our more naturalistic task, which involves the extraction of abstract latent features, revealing more typical processing of the sensorimotor system.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about why the current results differ from previous studies.

claim: The basic summary statistics of (macro-)saccades in the task (average size and inter-saccadic intervals) were similar to those found in natural vision.
source: Nevertheless, the basic summary statistics of (macro-)saccades in our task (average size and inter-saccadic intervals) were similar to those found in natural vision (Hayhoe et al., 2003; Land and Tatler, 2009), and there was a lack of adaptation to the task over the course of several days of free-scan sessions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental measurements to cited literature values.

claim: There was a lack of adaptation to the task over the course of several days of free-scan sessions.
source: Nevertheless, the basic summary statistics of (macro-)saccades in our task (average size and inter-saccadic intervals) were similar to those found in natural vision (Hayhoe et al., 2003; Land and Tatler, 2009), and there was a lack of adaptation to the task over the course of several days of free-scan sessions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by efficiency analysis across sessions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lack of adaptation and similarity to natural eye movement statistics suggest that participants did not depart dramatically from their natural eye movement strategies.
source: These seem to suggest, at least indirectly, that participants did not depart dramatically from their natural eye movement strategies.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the similarity of eye movement statistics to natural vision and lack of learning.

claim: The task focuses on the voluntary component of eye movements (scan paths of fixations) rather than the more involuntary processes of micro-saccades and drift.
source: Second, our task focuses on the voluntary component of eye movements, that is the scan paths of fixations, rather than the more involuntary processes of micro-saccades and drift (Rolfs, 2009; Ko et al., 2010; Rucci et al., 2007; Poletti et al., 2013; Kuang et al., 2012), which did not trigger new revealings.
evidence: The claim describes a design feature of the experiment and is supported by citations about micro-saccades and drift.

claim: In the task, involuntary processes are likely to be used for extracting information within each revealed patch, whereas high-level categorization required macro-saccades.
source: Importantly, in our task these involuntary processes are likely to be used for extracting information within each revealed patch, whereas high-level categorization required macro-saccades.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the role of different eye movement types in the task based on the spatial scales involved.

claim: The standard deviation of involuntary eye movements (0.22°) is similar to the Gaussian apertures used (SD of 0.18°), whereas the smallest length scale of the stimuli (0.91°) is 4 times larger.
source: This is because these involuntary processes cover an area with a standard deviation (SD) on the order of 0.22° (over the course of each fixation; Rolfs, 2009), which is similar to our Gaussian apertures (SD of 0.18°), whereas the smallest length scale of our stimuli (0.91°) is 4 times larger.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of measured values from the literature and experimental parameters.

claim: In natural scenes with finer structure, micro-saccades and drift may contribute more to abstract feature extraction.
source: However, it is possible that in natural scenes with finer structure, micro-saccades and drift may contribute more to abstract feature extraction.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about how the findings might generalize to different stimuli.

claim: Natural image statistics are often assumed to be spatially stationary on average but usually include local non-stationarities.
source: This is an approximation to natural image statistics that are often assumed to be spatially stationary on average (eg. Field, 1987) but usually include local non-stationarities (eg. different objects with different characteristic spatial frequencies).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about natural image statistics and is supported by citation.

claim: The stimuli were more naturalistic than many stimuli used in active sensing studies of visual search while still allowing rigorous control and measurement of information.
source: Nevertheless, our stimuli were more naturalistic than many of the stimuli used in active sensing studies of visual search (eg. simple 1/f noise) while still allowing a rigorous control and measurement of the amount of high-level category information available at any potential revealing location which would not have been possible with natural scenes.
evidence: The claim is a comparison of the current stimuli to those used in previous studies and an assertion about their advantages.

claim: The task limited the number of revealings in each trial rather than the time, although the temporal aspects of the eye movements (inter-saccadic intervals) were similar to eye movements with natural scenes.
source: Finally, natural vision works under time constraints. Our task limited the number of revealings in each trial rather than the time, although the temporal aspects of the eye movements (inter-saccadic intervals) were similar to eye movements with natural scenes.
evidence: The claim describes a design feature of the experiment and compares temporal aspects to natural vision.

claim: In a control experiment, the additional time allowed for rescanning the revealed locations did not affect the initial scanning strategy.
source: We also showed in a control experiment that the additional time allowed for rescanning the revealed locations did not affect the initial scanning strategy.
evidence: The claim is supported by the control experiment comparing participants with and without rescanning.

claim: It may be that participants are more efficient in naturalistic settings than the 70% found in the task.
source: It may well be that participants are more efficient in such naturalistic settings than the 70% we found in our task.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about how efficiency might differ in more naturalistic settings.

claim: By using a gaze-contingent display, the study was able to isolate the top-down strategies of eye movement selection.
source: First, by using a gaze-contingent display we were able to isolate the top-down strategies of eye movement selection, thereby complementing studies which examined the influence of low-level visual features and salience (Itti and Koch, 2000; Wismeijer and Gegenfurtner, 2012) on eye movement selection.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological contribution of the study and is supported by citations to related work.

claim: The task focuses on integrating low-level visual information into an abstract category, complementing studies that examine the effect of target value or more cognitive tasks.
source: In addition, our task focuses on integrating low-level visual information into an abstract category thus complementing studies that examine the effect of target value (Navalpakkam et al., 2010; Krajbich et al., 2010; Markowitz et al., 2011; Schutz et al., 2012) or more cognitive tasks that use eye movement (Nelson and Cottrell, 2007) or button-pressing for information search (Castro et al., 2009; Gureckis and Markant, 2009; Borji and Itti, 2013).
evidence: The claim describes a contribution of the study and is supported by citations to related work.

claim: Some previous studies used a similar Bayesian formalism to obtain active learning strategies specific to their tasks and showed that humans perform active learning when given the opportunity to consciously deliberate.
source: Some of these studies used a similar Bayesian formalism to obtain the active learning strategies specific to their tasks and showed that humans perform active learning when given the opportunity to consciously deliberate from which location in a scene they should gather information next.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from previous studies that are implicitly referenced in the preceding sentence.

claim: The work shows that high-efficiency active sensing is a natural strategy for eye movements that humans adopt without overt deliberation.
source: In contrast, our work shows that high-efficiency active sensing is a natural strategy for eye movements that humans adopt without overt deliberation, as evidenced by the inter-saccadic intervals matching naturalistic tasks and the fact that our participants reached near-asymptotic efficiency already in the first session of our task.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing natural eye movement timing and lack of learning effects.

claim: By using a pattern categorization task, the study could ensure that no single location was especially informative but that the task required an integration of information from multiple locations.
source: Second, by using a pattern categorization task we could ensure that no single location was especially informative but that the task required an integration of information from multiple locations both to select the next eye movement and to solve the task, and specifically that a closed-loop strategy was necessary for solving the task efficiently.
evidence: The claim describes a design feature of the experiment and its implications.

claim: Most previous studies have not addressed the important interplay between information gathering and fixation selection characteristic of naturalistic active sensing.
source: As such, most previous studies have not addressed the important interplay between information gathering and fixation selection characteristic of naturalistic active sensing: that, in general, the most informative location is ever-changing, dependent on the history of fixations one has already performed.
evidence: The claim is based on a review of previous literature and identifies a gap that the current study addresses.

claim: The formalism extends the range of active sensing to tasks which have arbitrary, not necessarily spatial, latent features (such as categories).
source: Third, in contrast to active sensing for simple visual search (Najemnik and Geisler, 2005; Navalpakkam et al., 2010; Morvan and Maloney, 2012), our formalism extends the range of active sensing to tasks which have arbitrary, not necessarily spatial, latent features (such as categories).
evidence: The claim describes a methodological contribution of the study and contrasts it with previous work.

claim: For the first time, the study provides a fixation-by-fixation analysis of information gathering under active eye movements by carefully matching the observer model to participants' performance.
source: In particular, it provides the first fixation-by-fixation analysis of information gathering under active eye movements by carefully matching our observer model to participants' performance.
evidence: The claim describes a novel contribution of the study.

claim: For the first time, the study was able to dissociate the contributions of the eye-movement selection process from those of perceptual, motor, and decision processes.
source: As a result, for the first time, we were able to dissociate the contributions of the eye-movement selection process from those of perceptual, motor, and decision processes, identify predominant sources of apparent sub-optimality in active sensing, and quantify the efficiency of choosing each individual fixation throughout scanning a whole scene.
evidence: The claim describes a novel contribution of the study enabled by the modeling approach.

claim: The approach is amenable to multiple tasks in different perceptual domains as well as high-level cognitive tasks.
source: Taken together, these features make our approach amenable to multiple tasks in different perceptual domains (Kleinfeld et al., 2006), as well as high-level cognitive tasks such as estimating the age or socio-economic status of people in a scene (Yarbus, 1967).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the generalizability of the approach, supported by citations.

claim: Three naive participants (aged 25–35 years) took part in the experiment.
source: Three naive participants (aged 25–35 years, none of them were authors or neuroscientists) took part in the experiment.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the experimental participants.

claim: All participants were neurologically healthy, had normal or corrected to normal vision and gave their informed consent before participating.
source: All participants were neurologically healthy, had normal or corrected to normal vision and gave their informed consent before participating.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about participant characteristics and ethical procedures.

claim: The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee.
source: The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about ethical approval.

claim: Each experiment took approximately 12 hr across 6 days (2 hr per day).
source: Each experiment took approximately 12 hr across 6 days (2 hr per day).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the experimental duration.

claim: Having two different types within the stripy pattern category ensured that the optimal scan path depended on the image.
source: Having two different types within the stripy pattern category ensured that the optimal scan path depended on the image (otherwise, always scanning in one direction where the length scales were different would be optimal).
evidence: The claim is a design rationale explaining why two stripy types were used.

claim: Categorization performance was perfect in training sessions for all participants.
source: The training sessions ensured that participants could learn the statistics of the image patterns. Categorization performance was perfect in training sessions for all participants.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about participant performance in training.

claim: All participants achieved an average performance of 70% accuracy or higher in free-scan familiarization sessions.
source: All participants achieved an average performance of 70% accuracy or higher.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about participant performance in familiarization sessions.

claim: The unknown, random stopping number of revealings served to encourage participants to be greedy in their information seeking.
source: The unknown, random stopping number of revealings served to encourage participants to be greedy in their information seeking.
evidence: The claim is a design rationale explaining the purpose of the random stopping rule.

claim: Saccadic variability and bias were included in the BAS model based on measurements made independently in a group of participants.
source: In order to take into account basic biological constraints on the accuracy of eye movements, we included saccadic variability and bias in the model based on measurements made independently in a group of participants which took into account both the standard deviation and bias of saccades both along and orthogonal (standard deviation only) to the desired saccade direction as a function of desired amplitude (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is a description of the modeling approach and is supported by measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Bayesian information criterion was used to compare models by controlling for their differing number of free parameters.
source: We used the Bayesian information criterion (computed across all participants) to compare the models by controlling for their differing number of free parameters and chose the best one (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is a description of the model selection approach.

claim: Once categorization choices were fitted, eye movements were predicted without any further tuning of parameters.
source: This meant that once we fitted categorization choices, eye movements were predicted without any further tuning of parameters.
evidence: The claim is a description of the modeling approach emphasizing that eye movement predictions were parameter-free.

claim: The critical features of the optimal solution were the relative locations of the revealings to each other due to the translationally invariant statistics of stimuli.
source: As the statistics of stimuli were translationally invariant, the critical features of the optimal solution was the relative locations of the revealing to each other.
evidence: The claim is an inference about what matters for optimality given the stimulus properties.

claim: For each trial, all revealing locations were shifted equally so that their mean was located at the centre of the image, thereby removing variability caused by which part of the image participants explored.
source: Therefore, for each trial we first shifted all the revealing locations in that trial equally so that their mean (centre of mass) was located at the centre of the image, thereby removing the variability caused by which part of the image the participants explored in that trial, which was irrelevant to optimality.
evidence: The claim is a description of the data analysis method.
